about.title: Anaheim Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Anaheim runs on people who work with their hands and on their feet. Hotel housekeepers, warehouse crews, theme-park staff, construction trades, delivery drivers moving along Ball Road and Lincoln Avenue — when one of them gets hurt on the clock, the first question is usually who pays for treatment and lost wages. In California, workers' compensation normally answers that, and it does so regardless of who was at fault. It is also usually the only claim you can bring against your own employer. What many injured workers in Orange County don't realize is that a separate claim may exist against someone else: a subcontractor on the same site, the owner of the building, the company that made a defective tool, or another driver who hit you while you were driving for work. Anaheim's public record shows 2,161 injury collisions in 2025, and a crash during a work-related drive is one way a third party enters the picture. LawProactive is free and independent. We connect you with an attorney who can sort out both paths, with no fee unless there is a recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Anaheim Workers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: Two Claims, Not One
items.desc: Workers' comp covers you regardless of fault, but it is usually your only remedy against your employer. An attorney can look for a negligent third party — a subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker, or another driver — who may owe you a separate injury claim.

items.title: Deadlines Handled Early
items.desc: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, and a third-party claim generally must be filed within two years. Getting connected quickly keeps both clocks from becoming a problem.

items.title: Protection Against Pushback
items.desc: Retaliating against a worker for reporting an injury is illegal in California. The attorneys in our network work on contingency, so you can ask questions about your rights without worrying about an hourly bill.

items.question: I was hit on SR-91 while driving for my Anaheim employer. Is that workers' comp or a car accident claim?
items.answer: It can be both. Because you were working, workers' compensation should cover your medical care and part of your lost wages no matter who caused the crash. Because another driver was involved, you may also have a separate injury claim against that driver, which can cover losses workers' comp does not. An attorney can coordinate the two so they don't work against each other.

items.question: Can I sue my employer directly for a workplace injury in California?
items.answer: Usually not. Workers' compensation is designed to be the exclusive remedy against your employer, even when the employer was careless. The exceptions are narrow, which is why attorneys focus on whether a third party — someone other than your employer — shares responsibility for what happened.

items.question: I didn't report my injury right away. Have I lost my rights?
items.answer: Not necessarily, but don't wait any longer. California expects you to notify your employer within 30 days, and reporting late can complicate a workers' comp claim. A third-party claim runs on a separate two-year deadline. An attorney can explain where you stand based on your specific dates.
